A 47-year-old female patient seeks medical attention for a 4-month history of anal pruritus. She
experiences straining with each bowel movement and describes a sensation of a protruding mass in
her rectum. She notes bright red blood on toilet paper after wiping but denies any abdominal or rectal
pain. Her medical and family histories are unremarkable for colorectal cancer. Physical examination
reveals normal vital signs and an unremarkable abdominal examination. Digital rectal examination
shows no blood, tenderness, or palpable masses. Anoscopic examination reveals a purple-blue mass.
What is the most probable diagnosis? Answer Choices: (A) Perianal abscess (B) Solitary rectal ulcer
syndrome (C) Anal fissure (D) Internal hemorrhoid (E) Anal fistula (F) Prolapsed internal hemorrhoid
(G) External hemorrhoid with thrombosis (H) Thrombosed internal hemorrhoid (I) Anal papilloma (J)
Rectal prolapse
 A. Anal fissure
B. Internal hemorrhoid
C. Anal papilloma
D. Thrombosed internal hemorrhoid
E. Prolapsed internal hemorrhoid
F. External hemorrhoid with thrombosis
G. Rectal prolapse
H. Solitary rectal ulcer syndrome
I. Anal fistula
J. Perianal abscess
